blocks.text: Chapter 8.
Set Tripwires — and Trust the Process
Last night with this book, friend — and it opens backstage at a rock concert, with a bowl of candy that saved lives.

Van Halen's touring contract contained a clause that became legend: a bowl of M&Ms in the dressing room — with every brown one removed. The press ran with it for years: spoiled rock stars, drunk on their own fame. But David Lee Roth was playing a much smarter game.

Pause and guess: Van Halen hauled NINE TRUCKS of complex staging into arenas that had never hosted anything like it — and buried in the contract's technical rider were safety-critical specifications about power, rigging, and floor loads. So what was the bowl of M&Ms actually FOR?
Ready? Here is what happened.

It was a tripwire for hidden negligence. Roth would walk into the dressing room and glance at the bowl: brown M&Ms present meant the promoter hadn't read the contract carefully — and if they'd missed the candy clause, what else had they missed? Girders? Amperage? The band would then line-check the entire production. A cheap, visible signal flagging an expensive, invisible problem, friend — set in advance, while everyone was still clear-eyed. And the opposite of a tripwire is the fate of Kodak: its own engineer built the first digital camera prototype in 1975; its own researcher warned in 1981 that digital would seriously threaten film within about a decade. Kodak had a ten-year head start... and treated it as ten years of permission to relax. That's the signature of gradual change, friend: no single day ever feels like the day to act. Film revenue stayed enormous, each quarter looked fine, and each year the company recommitted to the status quo without ever explicitly deciding to — until the stock fell from $94 to under a dollar, and bankruptcy came in 2012. Kodak didn't lack judgment. It lacked a low-fuel light: "if film sales fall 10% in any year, we convene and fundamentally reassess." A tripwire doesn't make the decision for you — it guarantees you notice a decision is needed.
Manufacturing the jolt

Humans can't feel a gradient, friend — so manufacture the jolt yourself. Deadlines are the most familiar tripwire, and they measurably work: in a Tversky-Shafir study, students offered $5 for a survey returned it 66% of the time with a five-day deadline... versus 25% with no deadline at all. Nothing about the task changed — the deadline simply created a moment when "later" was no longer available. Most of life's important work is deadline-free — career changes, hard conversations, strategy reviews — which means it loses by default. Give "someday" a date. Partitions work the same magic with resources: day laborers in India whose wages were divided into envelopes — some earmarked for savings — saved nearly double; opening a sealed envelope is a small conscious violation, and that flicker of awareness is the tripwire. (It's also why individually wrapped cookies survive longer than the open bag.) Venture capitalists partition by instinct: funding in tranches, each round forcing a fresh evidence-based decision. And here's the underrated second gift, friend: tripwires make risk psychologically affordable — "we'll try this until $50,000 or six months, then reassess" lets you act boldly inside the boundary instead of half-committing out of vague dread. Zappos even tripwires its hires: after training, new employees get "The Offer" — cash to quit on the spot — so staying stops being a default and becomes a choice.

Pause and guess: Not every danger announces itself with a number. Hospitals discovered patients often deteriorate for HOURS before a code blue — while junior staff hesitate to challenge the hierarchy. Their fix was a pattern-based tripwire. What was it, and what happened at Lucile Packard Children's Hospital?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Rapid-response triggers: pre-defined danger patterns — acute changes in heart rate or blood pressure, and crucially, the pattern "a staff member is worried about the patient" — that automatically authorize anyone, of any rank, to summon a rapid-response team. No permission needed; the trigger IS the permission. At Lucile Packard Children's, codes outside the ICU fell roughly 71 percent, and hospital-wide mortality dropped about 18 percent, friend. The pattern trigger does two jobs at once: it teaches people what danger looks like — and it grants the authority to act the instant they see it. Steal both halves for your own team: define the warning signs, including "someone is worried," and pre-authorize the escalation. And once the decision is made, make it stick with fair process — decades of procedural-justice research show people accept even unfavorable outcomes when they had a voice, felt genuinely heard, and got an honest explanation. The master stroke: restate the opposing case so well its advocates agree you've understood it — the Heaths describe a leader nicknamed the "velvet hammer" for exactly this. Two traps, friend: fake consultation after the decision is made is worse than none — people smell it; and answering pushback with advocacy hardens opposition, while genuine curiosity converts critics. A technically optimal decision the team quietly sabotages loses to a good decision the team owns. And the same mercy points inward: when you know your process was sound, you can stop relitigating the choice in your head.
The whole book in one breath

Eight nights, four villains, one process. Snapple taught us the empty chair — decisions fail by process, not analysis, and the spotlight never moves itself. Eisenhower priced a bomber in schools, and "whether or not" became a smoke alarm. Walton rode six hundred miles to copy a checkout line — multitrack real options, and someone has already solved your problem. The Vatican employed a devil's advocate for four centuries, and "what problems does it have?" beat politeness eleven-to-one. Seymour's base rates outvoted the room's confidence, the minivan drove fifty thousand miles, and Texas proved interviews measure nothing — zoom out, zoom in, then ooch. Grove walked out the door and back in; ten minutes, ten months, ten years all got a vote; Interplast named its customer. Taylor bought every pump in America because the future is a range — premortem the failure, preparade the triumph, pad like an elevator engineer, vaccinate with the truth. And tonight: tripwires against the drift that killed Kodak, brown M&Ms against hidden negligence, and fair process so decisions survive the people they touch. One breath shorter, friend: Widen. Reality-test. Attain distance. Prepare to be wrong. You cannot control outcomes — only how you decide. Being decisive is itself a choice.
The lantern by the door
That's Decisive, friend — Chip and Dan Heath, told fireside, eight nights. They'd want you to run WRAP on one real decision this week — not admire it on the shelf.

The embers settle, but look how the shelf has filled: Clear Thinking stands beside this one — the defaults and strengths beneath every decision; Thinking in Bets deals uncertainty like a poker hand. And lean in one last time, friend: the gas lamps of Baker Street are being lit as we speak. The detective's shelf is almost here.

Go gently. And tomorrow, pick one slow-moving risk in your life — and set its low-fuel light before you sleep: a number, a date, a threshold. Your future self, running on autopilot, will thank the clear-eyed you of tonight.
Key takeaways
Bad decisions are drifted into, not made: Kodak had the prototype, the warning, and a decade — but no tripwire to force the meeting.
Brown M&Ms: a cheap visible signal for expensive invisible negligence — design one for every partner and process you depend on.
Deadlines (66% vs 25%), partitions, and tranches convert "later" and lump sums into conscious decision points.
Tripwires make boldness affordable: act fully inside a pre-committed boundary instead of half-committing from anxiety.
Pattern triggers pre-authorize escalation — "a staff member is worried" cut codes 71% — teach the danger signs and grant the permission.
Fair process makes decisions stick, and trusting your own process quiets the relitigating: decisiveness is itself a choice.
